The question was: Who are the associates of Mr. Karadzic? And there was clearly a simple error of inserting the name "Karadzic," who cannot be an associate of himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Instead of the person that had been named earlier, Mr. Krajisnik. And I attempted in the most fair way to correct what was merely an error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I already related a bit the complaint by Mr. Stewart. Nevertheless, the question could have been put again to him and asked, listen well, and without mentioning that name, although that name was not such a surprise in view of the previous testimony just a couple of lines before. So I would say it's not -- the objection could certainly be of guidance for you to -- if you want to repeat the question, not then in the repetition to perhaps add something that was not in the earlier question that was misunderstood by the witness. And at the same time, it's not that of a surprise since the name was mentioned before. Mr. Egrlic, I would like to ask you the following: Before we had this discussion on what your first answer and what your second answer was, "president," "Presidency," in your first answer you said the following: "You see, I can see from the document that the --" no, I have got the wrong source now. When you were asked: "When you read the words 'order of the SDS Sarajevo', who did you think in the leadership of Sarajevo was ordering that this take place?" And then your answer was: "I thought that it was the - and we later clarified that - the president of the SDS, who had obviously discussed it with his associates and agreed on it." What made it obvious to you that he discussed this with his associates, especially in view of who you later named as being his associates? What made it obvious? Is it from the document, or was there any other reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I draw this conclusion based on the fact that in this document it says that under the leadership of Dr. Karadzic this meeting had been held. And a meeting implies that his close associates were present. And this also implies that members of the Presidency of the party were there as well as the representatives of the power from lower levels from the territories of municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is why I believe that all of them were somehow abreast of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document in its English translation says that an order was made public "At the meeting of all the municipal presidents on the 26th of October, 1991, chaired by Dr. Karadzic." In your answer, you referred to the -- you say the document says under the - as it is translated - the leadership of Dr. Karadzic. I take it that you refer to the chair of Dr. Karadzic over this meeting, as this document says. And you say: "A meeting implies that his close associates were present," whereas the document does not say any more than that this was a meeting of the municipal presidents. What makes you believe that a meeting of the municipal presidents would necessarily be -- would have been held in the presence of the other associates you mentioned, which I would say were of the central SDS level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In practice, it was known that the president of a party did not attend a meeting on his own, without his associates, and the title itself, "The order of the SDS Sarajevo," speaks for itself. It shows that the leadership of the SDS had agreed on this order and handed it down to the lower levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But these are two different issues. The one is who had previously agreed on the programme which was then made public in a meeting; and the second issue is who were present at that meeting. That's not the same. Let's start with the second part. You say it was publicly known, I think you said, that the president would not -- let me just try to find your words: "The president of the party did not attend a meeting on his own." Is that known for public meetings, for private meetings, for -- how was that known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant the system that was followed in the organisation of meetings. It would be normal to expect that the president, when it came to discussing such important issues, that the president would not be alone, that he would rather come accompanied by his closest associates, and that a meeting of this importance, where such important issues were discussed would be held in the presence of his associates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the inference you make. That's clear to me. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts. I put these questions because there has been a long examination on who exactly were the associates, where -- and of course I kept clearly in my mind that we need a factual basis for putting questions to a witness, especially if it comes to inferences, and it was, at least for me, totally unclear from a factual point of view and what's the use of further talking about things that have been repeatedly been presented to this Chamber if there's not the link with the special event we have in mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, you stated earlier that you knew the president of the Municipal Assembly, Mr. Banjac, very well from prior to 1991. During 1991, he was president of the Municipal Assembly and you were president of the Executive Board. Can you tell me how frequently you would meet with him.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We would meet almost every morning. The reason for that was the fact that we discussed our daily activities and we had our first cup of coffee together. And having this cup of coffee, we would discuss the activities that lay ahead of us on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: During the course of these morning-coffee sessions which you had on a daily basis throughout 1991, would you discuss with him the policies of your party and the policies of his party?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were different topics that we discussed. We had quite open discussions on all of the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I've finished with the document that we were looking at, so that can be returned. You stated that you had quite open discussions with him and that you discussed the policies of your respective parties. In the course of those discussions, did you gain an impression as to the extent of authority that Mr. Banjac had over the policy decisions made in Kljuc within the context of the policies that were set within his party?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know why Mr. Margetts adds on the last bit of the question, because it's completely unnecessary. The question could and should have simply stopped at "authority that Mr. Banjac had over the policy decisions made in Kljuc." We do invite Mr. Margetts to keep the questions at a minimum and not add anything which might be regarded as a pointer to where the question is going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, would you like to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It doesn't seem possible to me when you're talking about a leader of the SDS in a municipality to be discussing anything else when you're talking about the level of his independent authority than his authority within the context of the party. So whilst I accept Mr. Stewart's comment that the question could have Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond stood without that addition, it doesn't appear to me to either add or take away anything. And I'm quite happy for the question to proceed on the basis of what was his authority in respect of the policies set in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There are two aspects: First of all, if we're talking about policies, I think it would be fair to narrow them down so as to exclude at what time the garbage bins should be put out of the houses -- well, all kind of other matters, so to narrow that down. That is not necessarily done by referring to the party. You could name the issues or -- so therefore, I think to one extent I agree with Mr. Margetts that narrowing down the field of what could be covered by a question - I mean, policies could be a lot of other things as well - where we are focussing on certain matters of policy, I would say; on the other hand, not necessarily done by relating it to party issues. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I comment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts's response actually reinforces my point and makes it: That precisely because the context was clear, which I agree with - I agree with that comment of Mr. Margetts's; it didn't need saying - the difficulty is that if you then -- the damage has been done now, so I'm really making the objection because I want to signal it for the future --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- that by the time I object to the question, the damage has been done. The objectionable part of the question is there. To introduce something which is admittedly part of the clear context as a specific part of the question is capable of giving a pointer as to where the question is going and it should be avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- yes, I think I said that, that if you want to narrow down the issue in order to exclude all of the irrelevant things, that you should not do so, or as I said, not necessarily do that by referring to the party, because that's, of course, another issue. So to that extent, I think I partially agreed with your comments, and Mr. Margetts may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, during the course of 1991 when you had these daily meetings with Mr. Banjac, did you gain an impression as to what extent Mr. Banjac was able to make independent decisions?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: He could take decisions that fell within the scope of the president of the Municipal Assembly and decisions for which he had authority at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court what those matters that he had independent authority in regard to were.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Well, preparations for the Assembly for certain decisions that were to be discussed at the Assembly. This mostly had to do with tasks relating to the municipal administrative organ and to tasks relating to public utilities in the territory of the municipality. It also had to do with decisions relating to the economy, to the extent that the Assembly had influence on such matters. So these are the tasks dealt with at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try not to -- on the basis of the objection, I'm afraid that we are getting nowhere, because we're trying to circumvent that. Mr. Egrlic, you told us that you had -- you frequently had conversations with Mr. Banjac on a daily basis. We discussed a couple of minutes earlier the telefax or telex you had seen with instructions, that he -- were apparently sent by the SDS Sarajevo through the intermediary of Mr. Brdjanin. During your conversations, did you ever gain any awareness of Mr. Banjac being exposed to such instructions or guidance on other occasions than this specific occasion where you saw the telex?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I noticed towards the end of 1991 and at the beginning of 1992 that there were some very important issues in the territory of the municipality and that he wasn't able to deal with them on his own until he had consulted with the higher authorities. That is quite natural, since he personally had authority as president of the Assembly to deal with certain issues on an independent basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say "higher authorities," what kind of authorities you would have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when I say "higher authorities," I am referring to the higher authorities in Banja Luka. I have an example I can provide you with: When they decided to change the insignia on uniforms, given our different points of view, given that we were of the opinion that they shouldn't be changed until the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state was changed, they nevertheless proceeded to change these insignia. And finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm interested to know what authority was consulted, but perhaps you were just about to tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He confirmed with the leadership of the party and with the organs that had already been established in the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say "leadership of the party," did you mean at the regional level --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I say, Your Honour, with the utmost respect, although the Trial Chamber naturally has considerably more freedom, I suggest there should be limits to the extent to which questions from the Trial Chamber should lead. If that question had come from the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would have objected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I would undoubtedly have objected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Your Honour, with respect, I do present the same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I found it appropriate to consult my colleagues first before I would continue. You interrupted me, Mr. Stewart, when I said "leadership of the party." Did you mean at the regional level, the municipal level, the republican level? I wanted to open all levels. You then interrupted me and you objected. Could you tell us: When you said "the leadership of the party," what level you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I beg your pardon, Your Honour. I, with respect, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may later --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be too late. With respect, Your Honour, the reason I interrupted was precisely because the damage is done if I don't step in when I see the objectionable part of the question coming. And Your Honour, the same applies; and Your Honour, must, with respect, give me the latitude, please, as Defence counsel, to do that. I don't wish any discourtesy whatever in interrupting, Your Honour, and I hope that I would never do so unnecessarily. When I see that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness to take his headphones off. Could you please take his headphones. Do you read and understand English? Perhaps before -- do you read and understand English? Perhaps -- I'm sorry. Do you read and understand English? No? Then perhaps the witness could take his headphones off. Mr. Stewart, you're invited to say where you think I unacceptably leaded the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the reference -- Your Honour was -- it was clear. I was in fact right. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, whether you were right or not, I want to ask you where you think I leaded unacceptably the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, my comment that I was right was a lead-in to the point I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was an unnecessary lead-in. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I don't accept that, Your Honour. But with respect, I accept that ruling. I've said it now. When I interrupted Your Honour's question, Your Honour had referred -- I better be careful to make sure I've got it absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I'm not simply operating on fallible human memory. Excuse me, Your Honour. I have to lean over to the laptop here. Yes. Your Honour said, "When you said leadership of the party, did you mean at the regional level?" Now, Your Honour, I supposed at that point because of the tone of Your Honour's question and the way of which it was phrased, the question was inevitably going to go on into other possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And because it was clearly going to go on into other possibilities, I felt it was necessary for me to register my objection before Your Honour went into those possibilities, because those were the substance of my objection. So that is why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Stewart, if we're talking about the leadership of a party, it should be further identified - also in favour of the accused - what level that was. And I have carefully chosen not to start with the highest level and to say "the regional level," because on the basis of the information the Trial Chamber received until now, Mr. Krajisnik was not on the regional -- I would say the Banja Luka level but on a -- a higher level active in the party, and I carefully chose not to mention that first in order to avoid leading. I want you to know this. If you say "at what level," that would be -- would have been another way of dealing with that. By the knowledge the Chamber gained until now, we know that the SDS was mainly organised on the local municipal level, on the regional level, and on the highest, the state level. I wanted to make sure that -- to the witness what my question was about, including all possible levels, certainly not mentioning the level that many have said your client was at, to mention that first. Is there any need to respond? Otherwise, I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed there is, Your Honour. Because -- may I refresh my memory on the transcript after that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, then Your Honour said, "I found it appropriate to consult my colleagues first before I continue. You interrupted me, Mr. Stewart, when I said 'leadership of the party.' Did you mean at the regional level, the municipal level, or republican level. I wanted to open all levels. You then interrupted me and you objected. Would you tell us..." And then you ask the question, Your Honour: "When you said the leadership of the party, what level did you have in mind?" So in the preamble or the introduction to that question, Your Honour then did expound exactly that range of possibilities which was precisely the substance of my objection, and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What other levels would there be, as a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was unnecessary to state them, Your Honour, because whether they're presented in ascending order or descending order makes no difference. The presentation -- I would have objected if the Prosecution had put the question in that form, because it is precisely presenting the witness with, if you like, a menu of choices. The witness is a graduate engineer. The question "what level" is quite sufficiently comprehensible to this witness without having all the levels spelt out for him so that he can see which of the boxes he is required to tick in the course of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, what is a leading question? A leading question is a question which either suggests the answer to be given to that question or a question which includes a suggestion of something that exists which has not yet been established. If you say that this question was leading to the extent that it suggests that it should be the highest-step level, the medium level, or the low level, then you're right that it suggests one of these three answers. If you would say that the question suggests something that has not yet been established, which would be that there are these three kinds of -- three levels of -- three levels of leadership, I would say that the Chamber takes the position that these three levels as such have been established and are not without proper foundation. Let me -- give me one second to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The decision of the Chamber is that the objection is rejected. To the extent that there was any leading element in this question, it was not unacceptable, in the view of the Chamber. Could the witness please have his headphones on again. The Chamber at the same time conveys that even if mentioning a certain part in a question is not necessary, it's not therefore unacceptable to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I make it clear. I wouldn't go that far. I don't suggest that because a part of a question it is therefore leading. That would be an absurd proposition, and I don't put it forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, we're back with you. Mr. Egrlic, well, you've heard my question before. When you referred to the leadership -- but let me just try to find it again -- what did you have in mind? What level of leadership, as far as the party is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had the regional and central level in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Margetts, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, when you say "the central level," what do you mean by "the central level"?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean the Presidency of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. Would this be an appropriate time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This would be an appropriate time for a break. We'll have a break of 20 minutes. We'll resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we resume the examination of the witness, I have to correct one thing. Just before the break, I said that the Chamber rejected the objection, but there was no objection. There was just an indication of what the objection would have been if the question would have been put by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- sorry, that's -- perhaps I should make it clear. That's actually not my position, Your Honour. I would have -- I would have -- well, I want to make it clear, Your Honour. I would -- I started off by saying I would certainly have made the objection if the Prosecution asked the question. It was an objection, and I would wish it to be recorded and noted as an objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the objection -- then the objection is denied. The Chamber considered during the break another matter, and that is what are the limits of questions to be put by the Chamber. The Chamber certainly doesn't take the position that leading questions are excluded by all means if they are put by the Chamber, and it's also a matter of fairness of the examination which is at the top. Thirdly, the Chamber wanted to draw the attention of the parties to the fact that only in exceptional circumstances the parties should interfere when the Chamber examines a witness. And the Chamber is also of the opinion that the situation which had happened was not of such an exceptional character. Then, Mr. Margetts, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to show the witness the next exhibit, which is the exhibit dated 7 November 1991, translation ERN is 00568691.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, that would have number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P230 and P230.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, do you recognise this announcement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Are you the joint author of this announcement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was this announcement communicated to the citizens of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, can I -- I will refer to each of the paragraphs in this announcement in turn and I'll invite your comment in relation to them. The first paragraph I'll refer to is the second substantial paragraph on the first page under the heading "Joint official announcement." And I'll read that paragraph into the record and invite your comment. "In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the homeland of Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, one people - this time the Serb people - have decided to express their desire to break up Bosnia and Herzegovina in an unconstitutional plebiscite, contrary to the common will and interests of the others. Contrary to the will of the Parliament and based on the decision of the self-declared Assembly of the Serb People, established illegally, the Serbs and the SDS are, by this fact, expressing their will to break up Bosnia and Herzegovina, close themselves into strictly nationalist boundaries, and close the door to other peoples for the continued life together in a single Bosnia and Herzegovina." Mr. Egrlic, can you comment on that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: This announcement was issued with regard to the plebiscite of the Serbian people at which the Serbian people opted to remain within the former Yugoslavia, and our view of the matter has been expressed here. It was tantamount to breaking up the common State of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was an illegal act, given that according to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, proceeding in such a manner, which leads to breaking up the territory of the state, is unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Specifically you say that the Serbs wished to close themselves into strictly nationalist boundaries. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, may I just interfere for one second. The Chamber has heard quite some evidence on these plebiscites, and what -- and to what extent would it assist the Chamber to hear the -- I would say the personal appreciation of certain persons or even of a party on the local level? Would that really add something to what is at the core of this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this particular witness occupied a high-level position in the Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And had a very close association with the SDS leaders in that municipality. In this particular document in regard to the plebiscite, there is a clear expression by this witness of his contemporaneous opinion of the practical consequences that would follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why don't you then ask him about that. Practical consequences, fine. But your question was: Could you comment on the paragraph? And then we get a comment which is something totally in accordance with what a lot of other witnesses have told us before. So -- if you have specific issues, fine, but then focus on those. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I will proceed by directing your attention to specific parts of this document that are of interest to the Trial Chamber, and I will ask for your comment in relation to the practical consequences of these particular matters. In this first paragraph, you indicate that the direction that the SDS is taking by holding this plebiscite is intended to result in the Serbs closing themselves into strictly nationalist boundaries. Practically, how did it result in Kljuc, in terms of boundaries between the parties -- sorry, boundaries between nationalities?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: This plebiscite resulted in the situation in which only Serbs were asked to give their opinion on this issue. It was a mono-national plebiscite. We believed that would lead to the deprivation of other ethnic groups that resided in the area and the denial of their rights. That's why we didn't agree to this type of public expression on the status of ethnic groups in the former Yugoslavia, because Bosniaks expressed their wish to remain in the former Yugoslavia, however on somewhat different foundations, with a prior agreement with those who wanted to make up this new state. The organisation of a mono-ethnic state was perceived by us as a problem for other ethnic groups which might continue to reside in the area. We thought that their rights would be taken away from them and that that would mean the end of a possibility for them to continue residing in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I'd really like you -- we again got a general observation on the situation which is almost too well-known and has got nothing specifically with Kljuc. Please would you guide the witness in a more strict way to get additional information from Kljuc that you are seeking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I've finished with that document. Your Honour, I'd like to present the next document to the witness, that is, a document dated 24 December 1991, and the ERN for the translation is 00594891.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would then be number 231 for the original and 231.1 for the English translation?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I'm sorry. I beg your pardon, Your Honours. I certainly didn't wish to interrupt. Before we finally leave the previous exhibit, there's a rather strange but small point. But the previous exhibit, P230, at the very foot of the first page Your Honour will see the phrase "there would be no plebiscite" with an exclamation mark. Does Your Honour see that? It's the exhibit that we were just looking at a moment ago, 230. The joint official announcement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you show it to me? Because I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's in the -- I'm sorry, it's 230.1, I think, the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that says, "There would be no plebiscite."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just that that exclamation mark is just not there in the original. It's crept in. Sometimes punctuation does have a force. After all, that's why exclamation marks exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll get clarification for the exclamation mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And then Ms. Cmeric also points out to me that the italicisation of "Yugoslavia" has also been added somewhere. This is -- we don't know how all this happens, but -- it's unfortunate this that happenings, actually, but the same applies there. It's not italicised in the original. Somebody is tinkering a bit somewhere. I don't suggest it's the Prosecution; I'm not suggesting that, anything dastardly, but somebody is tinkering with these translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am even trying to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note these differences, but -- I don't know whether Mr. Stewart is linguistic expert in both English and B/C/S, but the person who has translated this is. And insofar as the italicisation and exclamation mark had been intended to be a clear translation of the intent expressed in B/C/S, I'm unable to comment one way or the other, other than to observe what Mr. Stewart has observed; that literally the printing is not the same in the English as in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not discuss this further. I think Mr. Stewart has drawn the attention again to a similar issue which I raised several times before. That means that the Prosecution is invited to look at whether it was proper or not and explain to the Defence, and if it's not proper, to present a new copy, a new English translation of the same document. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, do you have before you a joint official announcement dated 24 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this announcement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Are you the joint author of this announcement and was this announcement communicated to the citizens of Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In this announcement, you refer to a pro-war policy and the failure of the SDS to attend the interparty council. Can you comment on these matters.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: This information was a reaction to the security and political situation in the municipality during the time when this information was drafted. More specifically, it refers to the event or the incident that took place when the Serbian army units were departing for Croatia. They were lined up in front of the municipal building in Kljuc. They fired shots from various weapons and thus disturbed the citizens of the Municipality of Kljuc. It was also a reaction to the authorities turning the blind eye to such a situation and particularly to the fact that the SDS representatives did not participate in the multiparty council where this issue was discussed and where a solution was being sought for such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was it your impression that if the SDS had attended interparty meetings at that stage, the security situation in Kljuc would have improved?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: At that time, were the interparty discussions faltering?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: There were difficulties, and the work of the Municipal Assembly and its bodies also was faltering due to the deterioration of the security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: From the end of 1991 up until May 1992, how many Municipal Assembly meetings were there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. After the multiparty election and the establishment of the Municipality Assembly up to May 2000, there were a total of 14 sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In your previous answer, you referred to May 2000. Did you in fact mean May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: You're right. Between the 1st of January, 1991 until May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was there a Council for National Defence established in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It was established. According to the statute, this is a municipal body which is established and functions as a municipal body, and it consists of the people who occupy positions -- the positions of the president of the Assembly, the Executive Board, the Chief of Police, the Secretariat for National Defence, and a certain number of people who serve in the Assembly as representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In early 1992, how many meetings of this Council for National Defence took place in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1992 until May 1992, there were two such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did anything productive come from those meetings?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It was already the time when the political views were very different and the proposals advocated by the SDA, together with the MPs from the Municipal Assembly, did not take off the ground. The ones that did take off the ground were proposals of the SDS, who had a majority in that council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Whilst the joint bodies of the municipality were not meeting frequently in early 1992, did you, as president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly, continue to occupy an office in the same building as both Mr. Jovo Banjac and Mr. Veljko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I had my office there up to the 7th of May, 1992. It was in the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you continue to discuss matters relevant to the security situation and the government of Kljuc with them up until the 7th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes. But not as often as before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So instead of discussions on a daily basis, how frequently would you meet with Mr. Banjac in particular and discuss issues with him?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: During 1991, we had meetings on a daily basis almost. However, at the beginning of 1992, our contacts may have been once or maybe twice in a week. During the months of April and May, we only had one or two contacts altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egrlic. I've finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness the next document, which is a document dated 16 January 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the number would be, Mr. Registrar ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the numbers will be P232 and P232.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, have you seen this report before?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The report refers to a joint meeting of the MBO and the SDA held on the 14th of January, 1992. And I'd like to refer you to the paragraph that appears at the bottom of the first page of this report - that's in the B/C/S version - and it says: "The issue of our municipality topped the agenda at the meeting. Four speakers urged the Muslims to pay back the SDS in the same coin and form their own Muslim municipality in Kljuc." What steps did you take to form a Muslim municipality in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: We presented this idea at a meeting of the Municipal Assembly of Kljuc, and this happened once the Municipality of Kljuc was joined with the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina. The Bosniak people did not find their place in that decision. That is why we thought that the possible establishment of that municipality would result in the Bosniak people being given an area where they will be able to exercise their rights within the entire situation. However, this was just an idea which was never followed through, because there were no conditions in place for a referendum to take place and there were no conditions to hear the people's opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I refer you to the last paragraph of this document, and it specifically refers to a proposed referendum that was scheduled to take place on the 16th and 17th of February. That referendum did not take place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It is correct. The conditions for such a referendum were simply not in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you say "the conditions for such a referendum," are you referring to the security situation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the security and political situation in the municipality. We thought that this might cause dissatisfaction amongst citizens of other ethnic groups and that ultimately this could lead to the disruption of the security and political situation, which would get out of hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Egrlic. I've finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness the next exhibit, which is a handwritten diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would get, Mr. Registrar, number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be P233 and P233.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, can you open this diary and refer to the first entry, which is headed "Doboj, 5 February 1992." Mr. Egrlic, have you seen this entry for 5 February 1992 and had an opportunity to read it before today?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: The first time I saw this document was when I came here, to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, wouldn't it be a good idea to establish what the document is first, before we go into entries?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I took it that you would quickly do that, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, you have before you a handwritten diary which refers to various meetings of the SDS and other matters during the period 5 February 1992 through to 29 July 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are matters related to this diary that it would be better to deal with in private session, and if, Your Honour -- if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: To explain those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will go into private session. Closed session will not be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's confirmed on our screen. Please proceed. You can put your headphones on again, Mr. Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, could you refer to the first entry that is set out under the heading "Doboj: 5 February 1992." As you stated earlier, you've been given the opportunity to read this entry since you arrived in The Hague, and I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about it. Set out under this heading are four agenda items that were discussed at a meeting held in Doboj on 5 February 1992. The first item is a report from the expanded session of the SFRY Presidency. And if you look at the entry for item 1, it states that "Serbia's objective is to ensure that Serbs live in a single state, regardless of what it is called." Were you aware of this policy?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In Kljuc, what did you observe in respect of the implementation of this policy?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the political steps taken, all the political activities that were conducted - and to be more specific, activities that concerned the army and weapons - all these activities were in accordance with these ideas; that is to say, separation from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and annexation to the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Turning over the page, there's an entry under the heading "Item 2," which is headed "What stand has the SDS taken on Bosnia-Herzegovina?" Underneath the heading that says "The stand Karadzic and Krajisnik have taken," there is an entry, and it states: "Establish good coordination and firm organisation of the party, the police, the Territorial Defence, and the army." Can you comment on this particular objective. Mr. Egrlic, have you been able to find that entry? If not, I can give you some assistance.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: I haven't found it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It appears on the page marked "3 January."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts said in referring to this document, "Underneath the heading that says the stand Karadzic and Krajisnik have taken," the entry. Now, we've just quickly double-checked against the B/C/S version, which is obviously the original. Now, we stand to be corrected, but we don't read that as the following material being under the heading "The stand Karadzic and Krajisnik have taken." That doesn't seem to be the way it is set out at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to be the next item.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could have read the relevant line and then would have said that it's under item 2, the fourth or the fifth -- the fifth dot or the fifth line. Mr. Stewart is very much insisting, and I would support that, on as neutral as introduction as possible. It makes -- it doesn't serve any purpose here to mention the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, can you see the page which has the heading "3 January" and is marked with the identification marking 01399453? And can you see the item which is the second-last item on the page and appears at the lines which are marked "14, 15, and 16"? Can you read --

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and can you comment on whether or not this particular objective was implemented in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC
utterances.text: It says: "Establish real authority, especially in the Public Security Station, in the SDK, and the radio." It says: "Establish good coordination." This is a little unclear. And then it says: "The organisation of the parties, the police, the Territorial Defence, and the army." As far as these items are concerned, this had already been completed in Kljuc; this had already been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Looking at the clock, Mr. Margetts, since Mr. Hannis also needs five minutes. Mr. Egrlic, we'll conclude for today. We'd like to see you back tomorrow at 9.00, I take it in the same courtroom, Mr. Registrar. Yes. May I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have been giving today and the testimony still to be given, so speak to no one about your testimony. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Egrlic out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, there were two issues. I do understand that the CD-ROMs have been resolved by now and it was due to old hardware which could not take everything that was on the CD-ROM. So that matter has been resolved. The two remaining issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There was one other matter as I understood with regard to the CD, and that there was some difference between the translation -- or the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the issues we raised yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the subtitles. And I understand that apparently what has happened was that the B/C/S transcript was prepared from viewing the subtitles. The English transcript was prepared from listening to the audio. And so there's some slight differences. What we propose to do is prepare revised transcripts, match those up, and present them to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Wouldn't it be the best, since these subtitles could be read, if they're taken over in the B/C/S version, that we get a translation from that? Because there might be differences. It's not a very long text. So -- and then the same from what you hear that we get a B/C/S translation. So that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that we can do both versions then, Your Honour, and then we'll have both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because to make a merger might even cause more problems than we have already. Then the other issue was about --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- translations of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. One other matter before we leave the CDs. I also understand there was another issue about the time notations. That was difference on one transcript than the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe that -- again, that's a product of the translation being done from a different copy. We will get that synchronised so that there's one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, or no times at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or no times at all. With regard to the translation of documents, I understand one of those related to Exhibit 220, which was a diary of the witness, and at one point - I think on page 0200-5359, the English translation at 0301-4339 - There were quotations around a statement of -- taken from the diary which -- those quotation marks were not in the B/C/S. I can tell Your Honour that this was a CLSS translation. We will inquire with them about whether there is some sort of a translation protocol or something about written B/C/S from which that could be made, but we think that probably those translation -- those quotation marks should not be in there. But we have to follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally check and provide us new translation if they -- if they have to be taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then there was another issue or was that -- no, that was this morning about the date in the -- no, there was a date in a draft translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I don't have the answer to that one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So this resolves the matters of yesterday. Of course, a final decision has to be taken still on the admission of these documents. And it is in my mind that we decided once that we would take all the Sanski Most documents together. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just in relation to the question of the exhibits from yesterday. Of course, there's my outstanding objection in general to the transcripts of that particular video. There's the issue in relation to the translations that of course have been the subject of the discourse between Mr. Hannis and Your Honour. And, of course, just in relation to that -- the question of the diary, I think it would be more appropriate just to have the relevant page that the Prosecution relies on, rather than the entirety of Chapter 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis, you could give that perhaps some consideration, whether we could [inaudible] a little bit less diary than --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll consult and inform the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you could see what's relevant. Sometimes it's good to see the next date and the day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A bit of context, but perhaps not too much context.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then finally, I would like to make one observation. Yesterday the Chamber received a motion in relation to translations. This was, as I saw, a response to an invitation three months ago, and I also noticed that the Defence invited the Prosecution to respond within two days and to have a decision taken in two days as well. I don't know whether that time schedule after three months would be the one to be followed. Mr. Hannis, we'd like to hear from you tomorrow about when you would think that you could respond to that motion, which is a motion which, as is repeatedly said in the motion itself, does not always follow the -- well, let's say the mainstream of the ICTY case law. But still, especially if the Chamber has invited to follow under the specific circumstances of this case a different path, the Chamber would like to be thoroughly prepared for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn with again thanks to the interpreters, we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of July, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
